entries.source: Ludwig von Eyb der Ältere, Denkwürdigkeiten brandenburgischer Fürsten, ed. Constantin Höfler, Bayreuth 1849, pp. 129–130
entries.german:
Item herr sigmund von steten und Jorg von Rosenberg die einander ansprachen mit iren schriften die sich weit zugen, das sie bed die sach mit ritterlicher wer in schranken woltn austragn unnd sie bed, mein gnedign herrn Marggraf Albrechten baten, Ine schutz und schirm zu geben, des sich mein herr etlich zeit enthielt. Aber nach dem er von beden tailen und irer freuntschaft so hoch angesucht wurdt, sagt er jne zu schutz und schirm zu geben uff ainen nemblichen tag, den er Inn benennen wollt, das geschahe, das er In ain tag sazt.

Uff denselben tag bed taill mit ir freuntschaft komen und sonst vill ander von der Ritterschaft auß dem Fürstenthumb. Da wurd ein platz hie zu Onolzbach verschrankt unnd besezt, unnd ob tausend wepner zu fuß umb die schranken gestelt und in beden ain stund gesazt da sie zu den schranken solten eingelassen werden. des kam der ain von oben an in die schranken unnd der ander von unten auff in die schranken, das ir yeder inwendigs in dem Zirkel umbrait unnd das Volk bate Im syg zu geben, ainer anders dann der andere, darnach ruckt ir yeder an sain ort an die schranken gefast mit seinem spiess uff seine achselln die wurden angelassen dann das sie doch In Irem anrennen bede nichts schickten, Sonndern zur iren schwerten griffen und ein ander also ain gut weil uff dem platz umbtryben, da ward herr Sigmundts von steten hengst springen so hart das er in von Im sprang das Jorg von Rosenberg auch abfiel und sie bed zusamen lieffen und ain ander fasten zu Ringen, des Jorg von Rosenberg herr Sigmunden von steten Rugklin nider warff, auff in kom und in ansuchet mit seiner wer umb den sig des Connz von Luchau und herr hilpolt von hausen Als meins herrn Rete und grießwertl die horen und vernomen ob In baiden das sich herr Sygmund von steten begab und mein herr bed taill mit ir freuntschaft zu Tisch laden liess.
entries.english:
Sir Sigmund von Stetten and Georg von Rosenberg had exchanged extensive written accusations and both wished to settle the matter with knightly weapons within the barriers. They asked my gracious lord Margrave Albrecht for protection. He held back for some time, but after both parties and their friends pressed him, he agreed to grant protection on a day he would appoint. He set a day for them.

On that day both parties came with their friends, as did many other knights and nobles of the principality. A place here at Ansbach was enclosed and occupied, with more than a thousand armed men on foot stationed around the barriers, and an hour was appointed for the two to enter. One entered from above and the other from below; each rode around the circle and asked the people to pray for his victory, each in his own words. Each then went to his place at the barriers with his lance on his shoulder. They were let loose but neither accomplished anything in the charge. They took their swords and fought one another around the ground for a good while. Sir Sigmund von Stetten's stallion then leapt so violently that he fell off, and Georg von Rosenberg also fell. Both ran together and grappled; Jörg threw Sir Sigmund onto his back, came down upon him and pressed him with his weapon for victory. Kunz von Luchau and Sir Hilpolt von Hausen, my lord's councillors and marshals of the lists, heard and understood from both that Sir Sigmund von Stetten had submitted, and my lord had both parties and their friends invited to his table.

facts.content: fought Sigmund von Stetten in the lists at Ansbach, threw him down and prevailed when Stetten submitted.

entries.source: Jens P. Kleinau, “1478 A knightly duel”, Hans Talhoffer, 20 December 2011; summary of the article
entries.english:
Kleinau combines a detailed report associated with Duke Wilhelm of Saxony’s letter of 14 January 1478 with Ludwig von Eyb’s account. He calls Rosenberg’s opponent Simon von Stetten; Eyb calls him Sigmund. The following is a summary of Kleinau’s article, not a transcription of the historical report.

According to the article, Stetten reached Ansbach with 24 horses and Rosenberg arrived with his wife and 220 horses. Margrave Albrecht and his council tried to reconcile the parties. Their armour and equipment were inspected, and the swords were assigned by lot. Rosenberg entered the lists in a red silk gown, crossed himself three times and led his horse along the barriers. Stetten prayed at a church before entering.

Kleinau reports that Stetten publicly blamed Rosenberg’s pride, while Rosenberg said the quarrel arose because Stetten had captured a friend and dishonoured him; Stetten denied the allegation. In the mounted combat, the article describes the opponents striking with lances, losing shields and then fighting with swords. Stetten’s horse became unruly; Rosenberg seized Stetten and took his sword, but Stetten’s horse broke away and Stetten fell. Rosenberg also fell while trying to dismount.

On foot, Rosenberg prevented Stetten from taking a lance, and they struggled. Kleinau describes Rosenberg throwing Stetten down and threatening him with his sword; the officials intervened and the margrave ordered them separated. Rosenberg gave thanks, visited the church and returned to his lodging. Later he sent friends to claim a ransom of 200 gulden. Stetten acknowledged the debt but disputed when it should be paid; the margrave fixed a date, and the next morning the parties came to him for settlement.

The article dates the fight to 8 January 1478. Another chronicle places it on the day after Epiphany, 7 January; the day therefore remains uncertain in this record.

Later events: Kleinau states that Simon von Stetten later fought alongside Georg von Rosenberg in the feud against Bishop Rudolf of Würzburg and the counts of Hohenlohe. He attributes attacks or plundering to them at Hohebach, Mäusberg, Belsenberg, Steinbach, Ohrenbach, Amrichshausen and Jungholzhausen, and describes Rosenberg and Stetten as allies in a twenty-year feud with the counts. The article does not date these individual actions; they are later context, not events assigned to 1478.
